Hi Julia — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and the items we need to lock down so we can size an appropriate Redwood proposal: 

Summary of what you shared (please correct any mistakes):
- Primary use: patient-facing chat and guided triage with streaming responses and structured tool calls.
- Traffic pattern: steady baseline with short business-hour peaks. You expect simultaneous active sessions (streaming) during peaks of ~600–800 concurrent users.
- Latency SLO: 95th percentile for streaming token to first-byte target of <= 250ms; end-to-end prompt->final response ideally < 1.5s for short responses.
- Response shape: average 90–140 tokens per response, occasional long responses up to ~600 tokens.
- Daily tokens: ballpark 100k–250k tokens/day initially.

Open questions we promised to follow up on:
1) Confirm how you count "concurrent": concurrent live streaming sessions vs parallel API request concurrency.
2) Peak QPS (requests per second) and expected burst factor (we need 95th/99th peak numbers).
3) Connection model: do you plan to use long-lived connections (HTTP/2 streaming or websockets) or short-lived HTTP polling?
4) Any hard constraints around per-connection limit (e.g., share of connections from a single IP) or downstream firewalls that might close idle connections.

Next steps from Redwood:
- We will tee up an SE (Vivek) with a short architecture note and recommended rate-limit/concurrency configuration.
- We'll propose an interim hosted quota increase for your pilot and outline when Dedicated capacity is recommended.
- Please attach the SLO spreadsheet and any network topology diagrams (you mentioned a diagram that would help).

If the summary looks good, please reply with the clarifications above (especially confirmation of 600–800 concurrent streaming sessions and whether you expect bursts >2x baseline).

Thanks — talk soon.

—Marissa

Marissa / Aditya — quick architecture note and recommendation for Polaris based on Julia's numbers. High level first, then specifics and trade-offs.

Goal: meet 95th pct streaming-first-byte <= 250ms across peak concurrency ~700 and spikes to 1,000. Preserve token-cost efficiency and predictable tail-latency.

1) Connection model and pooling
- Recommend long-lived HTTP/2 connections with server push/streaming where clients can maintain persistent connections. Benefits: lower TLS handshake overhead, support for multiplexed streams (reduces per-connection limits), and easier backpressure.
- Client-side pool: keep ~8–16 connections per client host with HTTP/2 multiplexing. Each connection can multiplex multiple streams — recommended to limit to ~20 concurrent streams/connection to avoid head-of-line effects depending on client library.
- If clients cannot do HTTP/2, fallback to short-lived HTTP/1.1 with connection keep-alive and an internal connection pool of 50–100 per application server.

2) Redwood rate limits and quota model (hosted)
- Default hosted concurrency: 50 concurrent requests per API key. Default token throughput quotas are conservative for free/entry tiers.
- For production pilot we can provision a temporary hosted quota increase tied to the HubSpot deal (PL-67890) — bump concurrency per key to 200 and allowance for short burst factors of 3x sustained for 10 minutes, subject to monitoring.
- For steady-state at 700 concurrent streaming sessions, recommend Dedicated capacity. Hosted with per-key increases works for pilot but will be operationally fragile at 1,000 concurrent spikes.

3) Proposed Dedicated sizing (rough estimate)
- To satisfy 95th<=250ms with streaming and average 120 tokens/response, suggest starting with a Dedicated pool sized at ~4 GPU workers (NVIDIA A10/A30-class equivalent) with autoscaling headroom for short spikes. This assumes model optimized for streaming and quantized where appropriate.
- Dedicated gives per-tenant concurrency controls: you can reserve X concurrent streams and avoid noisy neighbors. Also unlocks higher per-key concurrency and predictable cost.

4) Backpressure & client-side queueing
- Implement a small local queue on the client side (capacity ~2–3 requests per user) with rejection codepaths and exponential backoff for retries. For streaming, prefer graceful degradation: fall back to shorter responses or a cached summary when the queue is full.

5) Observability & rollback
- Instrument token counts, inflight streams, tail latency (p99), and per-route queue length. Redwood Console can emit per-route token breakdowns and alert when quota consumption approaches 80%.

Immediate askable items I can put in the note to send to Julia today:
- Temporary hosted quota increase to concurrency per key = 200, burst factor = 3x for 15 minutes windows.
- Apply per-route priority for patient-facing streaming to favor these requests over lower-priority background jobs.

Risks / caveats:
- NAT and LB connection pooling by client infra can collapse many clients onto fewer sockets; we need to validate that the multiplexing settings are supported by their LB.
- Long streaming sessions increase token billing; confirm budget/expected spend.

If you want, I can turn this into a 1‑page PDF recommendation and an estimate of monthly cost for both the hosted-quota and Dedicated options.

—Vivek
